project: THE STOCK MARKET: FROM THE GROUND UP
company: Cyber Nexus Publishing / Crown & Lantern Press

items.title: Share volume and dollar notional trade volume are different measurements
items.specificTeachingObjective: Share volume counts shares; dollar notional multiplies each executed quantity by its own matched trade price.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: 600 shares printed at $12.00 and 400 at $12.50 imply 1,000 traded shares but $7,200+$5,000=$12,200 of total print notional.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Is 300 shares the same as $2,900 notional?
items.correction: Sum each reported share quantity times its own executed print price; report shares and dollars separately.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake to avoid: A real trader can confuse 1,000 shares with $1,000 of turnover and compare two securities with incompatible quoted prices. The correct response is to verify the inputs and acknowledge uncertainty rather than invent a fill or future evidence.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: 100 shares at $9 and 200 at $10 imply 300 shares and $2,900 notional; identify the separate units. Explain the calculation and what a previously unavailable price or document would change.
items.riskBoundary: HLC3 bar approximation cannot substitute for exact print notional.

items.title: Market capitalization reflects a quote multiplied by shares outstanding, not cash in the company
items.specificTeachingObjective: Market capitalization is an equity market-value estimate based on share price and the selected outstanding-share count.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Five million outstanding shares at $20 each imply $100 million equity market capitalization, not $100 million in company cash.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Does $100 million market cap imply $100 million cash held?
items.correction: Multiply current quote by current eligible shares outstanding, then distinguish equity value from corporate cash.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake to avoid: A beginner may treat market capitalization as a treasury account balance rather than a price-dependent estimate of common equity value. The correct response is to verify the inputs and acknowledge uncertainty rather than invent a fill or future evidence.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: Three million common shares at a $40 quote imply a $120 million market capitalization; identify what is not measured. Explain the calculation and what a previously unavailable price or document would change.
items.riskBoundary: Market capitalization can change without cash entering the firm.

items.title: An assumed public float is not identical to a company total outstanding share count
items.specificTeachingObjective: Shares outstanding and an estimated publicly tradable float measure different groups of shares and depend on definitions.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Of 10 million outstanding common shares, assume exactly 2 million are excluded by the exercise float definition; modeled float is 8 million.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Can insider holdings alone establish public float?
items.correction: Identify which shares are excluded under the declared float methodology and date.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake to avoid: Treating every non-institutional share as available float or assuming float equals all shares can misstate a market-liquidity screen. The correct response is to verify the inputs and acknowledge uncertainty rather than invent a fill or future evidence.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: Of 15 million outstanding shares, 4 million are assumed excluded under a declared rule; estimate modeled float and name one unknown. Explain the calculation and what a previously unavailable price or document would change.
items.riskBoundary: Float differs by vendor and cannot prove immediately available liquidity.

items.title: A quoted spread percentage depends on the reference price used in its denominator
items.specificTeachingObjective: The quoted bid-ask spread in dollars can be divided by the simultaneous midpoint to express a relative spread for teaching.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Bid $10.00 and ask $10.10 give midpoint $10.05, width $0.10 and a midpoint-relative width of about 0.995%.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Why is a 10-cent spread relative to $10.05 about 0.995%?
items.correction: Use same-time bid and ask, midpoint denominator and quoted width.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake to avoid: A trader who mixes quote times or divides by the wrong benchmark can report an apparently precise but meaningless spread percent. The correct response is to verify the inputs and acknowledge uncertainty rather than invent a fill or future evidence.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: A $20.00 bid and $20.20 ask imply midpoint $20.10 and relative quoted spread about 0.995%. Explain the calculation and what a previously unavailable price or document would change.
items.riskBoundary: Quoted spread is not actual effective spread.

items.title: The same one-cent price change has a different percentage significance at different prices
items.specificTeachingObjective: A fixed-dollar movement should be compared with the starting price before interpreting relative magnitude.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: A $0.01 increase from $5.00 equals 0.20%, while the same $0.01 increase from $50.00 is 0.02%.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Does a cent move mean the same return on $5 and $50?
items.correction: Divide the same dollar change by each starting price.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake to avoid: Comparing pennies alone across two share-price levels can make a minor percentage change appear as important as a major one. The correct response is to verify the inputs and acknowledge uncertainty rather than invent a fill or future evidence.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: Compare a $0.02 rise from $10.00 with a $0.02 rise from $100.00 as percentages. Explain the calculation and what a previously unavailable price or document would change.
items.riskBoundary: Equal absolute moves differ in relative return.

items.title: Basis points convert a defined percentage change into hundredths of one percent
items.specificTeachingObjective: One basis point is one hundredth of one percentage point and can express price or rate changes with declared context.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: A price rises from $50.00 to $50.25; 0.25/50×100=0.50%, which is 50 basis points.
items.diagnosticQuestion: How many signed basis points is −0.50%?
items.correction: Multiply the signed percentage by 100 to obtain −50 bp.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake to avoid: Calling a 50-basis-point price increase 50% or $0.50 can produce a hundredfold position-analysis error. The correct response is to verify the inputs and acknowledge uncertainty rather than invent a fill or future evidence.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: A price falls from $80 to $79.60; express the signed percentage change and basis points. Explain the calculation and what a previously unavailable price or document would change.
items.riskBoundary: Price bp are not yield bp.

items.title: Average entry price must weight each partial purchase by its share count
items.specificTeachingObjective: A simple arithmetic average of different execution prices is wrong when share quantities differ.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Buying 20 shares at $10 and 30 at $11 produces (200+330)/50=$10.60 per share, not an unweighted $10.50.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Why can unequal fills not be averaged simply?
items.correction: Weight each confirmed fill by executed shares; exclude outstanding quantity.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake to avoid: A trader may average two execution prices without weighting them and record a false break-even reference for the position. The correct response is to verify the inputs and acknowledge uncertainty rather than invent a fill or future evidence.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: Buy 10 shares at $8 and 15 at $9; compute the quantity-weighted average without fees. Explain the calculation and what a previously unavailable price or document would change.
items.riskBoundary: Fee-adjusted cost basis can differ.

items.title: Cash available and purchase price place an arithmetic ceiling on whole-share quantity
items.specificTeachingObjective: Cash-funded whole-share quantity is limited by affordable purchase cost when fees and trading restrictions are separately addressed.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: With $500 cash and a hypothetical $12.30 per-share execution price, 40 whole shares cost $492, leaving $8 before any charges.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Can $500 buy 41 whole shares at $12.30?
items.correction: Floor cash divided by assumed per-share execution price and recheck charges.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake to avoid: Rounding a calculated quantity upward can create an order larger than available funds even before commission or price movement. The correct response is to verify the inputs and acknowledge uncertainty rather than invent a fill or future evidence.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: With $125 cash and a $9.40 assumed execution, calculate the maximum whole shares and unused cash. Explain the calculation and what a previously unavailable price or document would change.
items.riskBoundary: Market-order fills need not match a stale quote.

items.title: Fractional-share quantity is not automatically rounded to a whole share
items.specificTeachingObjective: When a broker supports it, a notional-dollar order can correspond to part of a share rather than a full integer quantity.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: A $25 notional purchase at an assumed $40-per-share fill would buy 0.625 shares before any account restrictions or charges.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Does $25 at $40 necessarily fill one whole share?
items.correction: Calculate 0.625 theoretical shares and check fractional eligibility.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake to avoid: Students may assume fractions are always permitted or incorrectly round 0.625 to one whole share and overstate purchasing power. The correct response is to verify the inputs and acknowledge uncertainty rather than invent a fill or future evidence.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: Compute the theoretical shares for a $30 notional purchase at $48 per share and note broker availability. Explain the calculation and what a previously unavailable price or document would change.
items.riskBoundary: Theoretical quantity does not establish execution.

items.title: A two-for-one split changes nominal shares and per-share price without automatically creating wealth
items.specificTeachingObjective: In an idealized 2-for-1 stock split, the share count doubles while the comparable per-share price halves at the split adjustment.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Forty shares at $100 represent $4,000; an illustrative 2-for-1 adjustment gives 80 shares at $50, still $4,000.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Does a 2-for-1 split create a mechanical 100% gain?
items.correction: Double quantity and halve the split-adjusted reference price.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake to avoid: A shareholder may mistake twice as many shares for twice the wealth, ignoring the associated mechanical price-scale change. The correct response is to verify the inputs and acknowledge uncertainty rather than invent a fill or future evidence.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: Convert 25 shares at $80 through a hypothetical 2-for-1 split and compare modeled position values. Explain the calculation and what a previously unavailable price or document would change.
items.riskBoundary: Actual repricing and distribution terms can differ.

items.title: A reverse split changes share quantity and the comparable price scale
items.specificTeachingObjective: In a simplified reverse split, shares decrease by a stated ratio while an adjusted reference price increases correspondingly.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: A holder of 120 shares at $2.00 has $240 of position value; a 1-for-10 reverse split implies 12 shares at an adjusted $20.00 reference.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Why is a tenfold reverse-split quote not a tenfold gain?
items.correction: Divide quantity by ten and multiply reference price by ten.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake to avoid: A trader may infer profit from a tenfold price display increase while overlooking that the share count fell by the same factor. The correct response is to verify the inputs and acknowledge uncertainty rather than invent a fill or future evidence.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: Convert 80 shares at $3 through a hypothetical 1-for-4 reverse split and compare values. Explain the calculation and what a previously unavailable price or document would change.
items.riskBoundary: Cash in lieu and market repricing can change outcomes.

items.title: Split-adjusted and unadjusted prices cannot be mixed in a simple return comparison
items.specificTeachingObjective: A split can change the nominal quote scale without a comparable change in the economic value of an existing share position.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: A prior $80 close is $40 on a 2-for-1 adjusted basis; an adjusted next $42 close represents +5%, not an unadjusted −47.5%.
items.diagnosticQuestion: How should pre-split $80 be compared with post-split $42?
items.correction: Adjust earlier $80 to $40 under 2-for-1 then compute 5% return.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake to avoid: A student may label a mechanical split price change a crash when a chart combines adjusted and raw price scales. The correct response is to verify the inputs and acknowledge uncertainty rather than invent a fill or future evidence.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: After a 4-for-1 split, compare a previous $120 close with a next $31 comparable close as adjusted price return. Explain the calculation and what a previously unavailable price or document would change.
items.riskBoundary: Never mix adjustment states across timestamps.

items.title: An earlier displayed ask is not a confirmed market-order purchase price
items.specificTeachingObjective: An observed quote and a subsequent execution can differ because displayed liquidity and market conditions change.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: A quote showed ask $10.50, but a later 100-share market buy filled at $10.70; paid notional was $1,070, $20 above the earlier ask-based estimate.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Does an earlier $10.50 ask prove a later market fill at $10.50?
items.correction: Use actual 100-share fill at $10.70; earlier ask is context.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake to avoid: Treating the first quoted ask as a guaranteed buy fill can understate the actual money committed or the trade's cost. The correct response is to verify the inputs and acknowledge uncertainty rather than invent a fill or future evidence.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: The earlier ask is $8.00 and 50 shares fill at $8.12; calculate the difference from the earlier quote reference. Explain the calculation and what a previously unavailable price or document would change.
items.riskBoundary: A quote is not a trade confirmation.

items.title: A buy limit places a price boundary without guaranteeing an execution
items.specificTeachingObjective: An eligible buy-limit order can execute at its limit price or better, but the order may remain unfilled.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: A $20.00 buy limit is below the visible $20.30 offer; the displayed quote alone establishes neither a fill nor a no-fill result for the order even if a later candle trades $19.90.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Does a later $19.90 candle low prove a $20 limit filled?
items.correction: Require order status, marketable liquidity, queue and actual trade confirmation.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake to avoid: Marking a paper order as filled merely because a chart's later low touched its limit creates look-ahead and false execution history. The correct response is to verify the inputs and acknowledge uncertainty rather than invent a fill or future evidence.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: A $15.00 buy limit sits below a $15.25 offer; identify the missing information needed to establish a fill. Explain the calculation and what a previously unavailable price or document would change.
items.riskBoundary: A prior quoted offer cannot prove a fill or zero fills.

items.title: Multiple partial executions require a weighted average fill price
items.specificTeachingObjective: A single submitted order can receive different partial fills and the average is based on actual executed share quantities.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Forty shares filled at $10.00 and sixty at $10.20; 100 shares executed at a weighted $10.12 average.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Should unfilled shares count in the weighted average?
items.correction: Weight only actual fills by executed quantities.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake to avoid: A trader who divides the executed dollar total by submitted rather than executed shares reports a misleading average fill. The correct response is to verify the inputs and acknowledge uncertainty rather than invent a fill or future evidence.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: Thirty shares fill at $5.10 and twenty fill at $5.20; calculate the average price for 50 executed shares. Explain the calculation and what a previously unavailable price or document would change.
items.riskBoundary: Future fills may alter the average.

items.title: Candlestick body height and high-to-low range measure different amounts
items.specificTeachingObjective: A candle body measures the absolute difference between open and close, while its total range includes intrabar extremes.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Open $20, close $20.80, high $21, low $19.50 give body $0.80 and full range $1.50; body is 53.33% of range.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Can a single candle show who initiated every trade?
items.correction: Compute abs(close−open)/(high−low) for completed, nonzero-range OHLC only.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake to avoid: A student who treats a wide upper wick as body movement may misread the candle's open-to-close relationship. The correct response is to verify the inputs and acknowledge uncertainty rather than invent a fill or future evidence.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: Open $30, close $29.40, high $30.40, low $29; calculate body percentage of full range. Explain the calculation and what a previously unavailable price or document would change.
items.riskBoundary: Body ratio does not encode intrabar sequence.

items.title: Upper and lower candlestick wicks use the body endpoints as boundaries
items.specificTeachingObjective: A completed candle's upper wick extends from its higher open/close endpoint to the high; its lower wick extends from the low to the lower endpoint.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Open $10, close $10.60, high $11.20, low $9.80 give upper wick $0.60 and lower wick $0.20.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Does a long upper wick prove sellers traded last?
items.correction: Upper=high−max(open,close); lower=min(open,close)−low.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake to avoid: A trader who always subtracts the close from the high can miscalculate the upper wick for a bearish candle. The correct response is to verify the inputs and acknowledge uncertainty rather than invent a fill or future evidence.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: Open $20, close $19.50, high $20.50, low $19.00; compute upper and lower wicks separately. Explain the calculation and what a previously unavailable price or document would change.
items.riskBoundary: Wick cannot prove order sequencing or reversal.

items.title: An opening price gap compares two different confirmed observations
items.specificTeachingObjective: An open-to-prior-close gap measures the current session opening value relative to a previous eligible completed close.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: An earlier completed closing print at $50 and the new session's opening print at $51.20 imply an opening gap of $1.20, or +2.40%.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Can after-hours price substitute for regular-session close in a gap?
items.correction: Declare sessions and eligible price types before comparing.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake to avoid: Comparing a new regular open to an unadjusted pre-split close or an unrelated after-hours quote creates a false gap. The correct response is to verify the inputs and acknowledge uncertainty rather than invent a fill or future evidence.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: Compare a $24.00 prior regular-session close with a $23.40 next regular-session open as dollars and percent. Explain the calculation and what a previously unavailable price or document would change.
items.riskBoundary: Corporate adjustments and opening eligibility affect gaps.

items.title: A five-minute bar's opening timestamp does not reveal its completed candle at that instant
items.specificTeachingObjective: Bar timestamps often identify the beginning of an interval; the complete interval's high, low, close and volume become known only after observation.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: A bar labeled 09:30 covers 09:30–before 09:35 in an opening-time convention; its final high at 09:34 cannot be used by a 09:31 decision.
items.diagnosticQuestion: At 09:31 is the bar labeled 09:30 through 09:35 fully known?
items.correction: No; its final high/low are unknown until completed and disseminated.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake to avoid: A chart lesson that shows the eventual 09:30 bar high at 09:31 silently trains decisions using future information. The correct response is to verify the inputs and acknowledge uncertainty rather than invent a fill or future evidence.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: At 10:02 during a bar labeled 10:00, identify which five-minute bars are fully completed and which high is unknown. Explain the calculation and what a previously unavailable price or document would change.
items.riskBoundary: Replay cutoff must use actual observation availability.

items.title: Relative volume requires matched time windows rather than mismatched daily totals
items.specificTeachingObjective: Volume comparison is meaningful only after defining the same duration, session conditions and population for the baseline and observed period.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Five thousand shares in the first ten completed minutes versus a 4,000-share mean for comparable ten-minute windows equals 1.25× relative volume.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Can first 10-minute volume be divided by a daily mean to call RVOL high?
items.correction: Use corresponding ten-minute historical windows with positive denominator.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake to avoid: A trader may interpret an apparently high relative-volume number caused only by a shorter or otherwise mismatched comparison window. The correct response is to verify the inputs and acknowledge uncertainty rather than invent a fill or future evidence.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: Six thousand shares in the first completed fifteen minutes versus a historical 8,000-share matched-window baseline yields what ratio? Explain the calculation and what a previously unavailable price or document would change.
items.riskBoundary: Mismatched windows can manufacture a false high ratio.

items.title: Position weight measures one holding's value relative to the whole portfolio
items.specificTeachingObjective: A position weight compares that holding's marked value with total current portfolio value, using the same valuation timestamp.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: 40 shares marked at $25 are worth $1,000 in a $5,000 portfolio; that holding is 20% of marked portfolio value.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Is share quantity divided by portfolio dollars a valid weight?
items.correction: Convert the holding to same-time market value first, then divide by total net portfolio value.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake: A trader may wrongly divide share count by dollar portfolio value and misstate concentration. Correct it by declaring the missing information and using only completed, reported evidence rather than inventing a fill.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: 30 shares at $18 in a $3,600 portfolio represent what percentage of marked value? Explain the relevant units, what is only assumed, and what would invalidate your result.
items.riskBoundary: Same-time valuations and included account liabilities must be defined.

items.title: Uninvested cash contributes to the portfolio allocation denominator
items.specificTeachingObjective: A portfolio allocation percentage should account for relevant uninvested cash rather than pretending the portfolio contains only securities.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: A $3,000 stock position plus $2,000 cash makes $5,000 portfolio value; the cash allocation is 40%.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Should uninvested cash be omitted from portfolio allocation?
items.correction: Include eligible cash with marked holdings in total net equity; distinguish restricted buying power.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake: A trader may omit idle cash and accidentally call a partial equity allocation a fully invested portfolio. Correct it by declaring the missing information and using only completed, reported evidence rather than inventing a fill.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: A $7,500 stock position and $2,500 cash create what cash weight, ignoring fees and borrowing? Explain the relevant units, what is only assumed, and what would invalidate your result.
items.riskBoundary: Cash weight is not necessarily withdrawable or available-to-trade cash.

items.title: Adding cash changes investment weights without a market-price change
items.specificTeachingObjective: A cash contribution raises the total portfolio denominator even if every stock quote stays exactly where it was.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: $4,000 in stock and $1,000 cash make an 80% stock weight; adding $1,000 cash without trading changes stock weight to $4,000/$6,000 = 66.67%.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Does a cash contribution change weight even if market prices stay flat?
items.correction: Recompute the larger total account denominator after the contribution before discussing positions.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake: A trader can misreport deposit-funded account growth as successful trading performance. Correct it by declaring the missing information and using only completed, reported evidence rather than inventing a fill.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: $3,000 stock plus $1,000 cash receives an extra $2,000 contribution; find the new stock weight. Explain the relevant units, what is only assumed, and what would invalidate your result.
items.riskBoundary: Contribution is an external flow, not a generated trading gain.

items.title: An initial deposit is not the same as the account's current marked equity
items.specificTeachingObjective: A deposit records capital contributed; marked equity adds current marked investment changes and relevant other account components.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: An investor deposits $2,000 and the held securities subsequently lose $120 while no other items change; account marked equity is $1,880, not $2,000.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Does an initial $2,000 deposit force current equity to remain $2,000?
items.correction: Update marked assets and liabilities as of now; a $120 loss yields $1,880 in the simplified case.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake: A trader may call the original deposit their available account value after the market has moved. Correct it by declaring the missing information and using only completed, reported evidence rather than inventing a fill.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: Starting equity of $4,500 falls $225 in marked securities value with no transfers; what is current equity? Explain the relevant units, what is only assumed, and what would invalidate your result.
items.riskBoundary: Net liquidation and cash balances may differ.

items.title: Investment return differences in percentage points are not percentage changes of the return itself
items.specificTeachingObjective: A percentage-point gap is obtained by subtracting two stated percentages measured on a compatible period and basis.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: A portfolio gains 8% and a compatible benchmark gains 5% over the same interval; the portfolio is ahead by 3 percentage points.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Is an 8% minus 5% performance difference 3% relative return?
items.correction: Report 3 percentage points for the difference; relative return requires its own defined ratio.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake: A learner may call a 3-point difference a 60% gain without explaining the benchmark denominator. Correct it by declaring the missing information and using only completed, reported evidence rather than inventing a fill.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: A portfolio returns −2% while the benchmark returns +1% over the same dates; what is the percentage-point gap? Explain the relevant units, what is only assumed, and what would invalidate your result.
items.riskBoundary: A percentage-point difference is not automatically risk-adjusted alpha.

items.title: Sequential percentage changes compound rather than simply adding together
items.specificTeachingObjective: A later percentage return applies to the already changed value, so the base for each period can differ.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: A $100 holding rises 10% to $110 and then falls 10% to $99; the two-period net change is −1%, not zero.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Can +10% and −10% be added to conclude no change?
items.correction: Compound gross factors 1.10 × .90 = .99, a net −1%.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake: A trader may add plus and minus percentages and wrongly conclude the position returned to the starting value. Correct it by declaring the missing information and using only completed, reported evidence rather than inventing a fill.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: A fictional holding rises 20% in one completed period and falls 10% in the next; find its total return. Explain the relevant units, what is only assumed, and what would invalidate your result.
items.riskBoundary: Fee, dividend and cash-flow assumptions must be stated.

items.title: Return on an invested slice is not automatically a return on the entire portfolio
items.specificTeachingObjective: A position-specific return and portfolio-level return use different denominators when a portfolio includes cash or other holdings.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: A $1,000 holding gains $100 while a separate $4,000 stays in cash; the holding gains 10%, but the combined $5,000 account gains 2% before fees.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Can a 10% gain on $1,000 imply 10% gain on a $5,000 account?
items.correction: Divide $100 change by the relevant $5,000 total to show 2% account return.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake: A trader may report a successful single-position percentage as the whole-account investment result. Correct it by declaring the missing information and using only completed, reported evidence rather than inventing a fill.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: A $600 invested holding earns $30 while $2,400 remains in cash; compute holding return and total-account return. Explain the relevant units, what is only assumed, and what would invalidate your result.
items.riskBoundary: Match dates and control for external deposits.

items.title: Gross sales proceeds and deposited net proceeds are different amounts
items.specificTeachingObjective: The dollars generated by shares multiplied by execution price can exceed the account's after-fee sales proceeds.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Selling 30 shares at $18 generates $540 gross proceeds; a fictional $2 selling fee makes $538 net proceeds before tax.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Does $540 gross sale automatically become $540 cash credit?
items.correction: Subtract the stated $2 selling charge: $538 fictional net proceeds before tax.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake: A learner may label the entire sale notional as profit rather than proceeds. Correct it by declaring the missing information and using only completed, reported evidence rather than inventing a fill.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: Sell 25 shares at $12.50 with a $1.50 selling fee; calculate gross and net proceeds. Explain the relevant units, what is only assumed, and what would invalidate your result.
items.riskBoundary: Sales proceeds and capital gain require different denominators.

items.title: Gross dividend entitlement and after-withholding cash can differ
items.specificTeachingObjective: A quoted cash dividend is a declared per-share amount, but any fictional withholding reduces cash actually received.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Eligible 100 shares at $0.30 dividend imply $30 gross; a fictional 10% withholding leaves $27 net cash.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Does $30 gross dividend mean $30 after withholding?
items.correction: Apply the explicitly hypothetical 10% withholding separately to reach $27 cash.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake: A trader can confuse the declared per-share dividend with guaranteed after-tax cash. Correct it by declaring the missing information and using only completed, reported evidence rather than inventing a fill.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: Assume 80 entitled shares, $0.25 per share and a hypothetical 5% withholding; find gross and net amounts. Explain the relevant units, what is only assumed, and what would invalidate your result.
items.riskBoundary: Tax rules cannot be inferred from an invented rate.

items.title: A trading settlement interval counts eligible business days, not calendar days
items.specificTeachingObjective: For a transaction under a stated T+1 convention, the next eligible business day follows the trade date under the governing calendar.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: With no holidays, a Friday regular-way U.S. stock transaction under an assumed T+1 calendar settles Monday, not Saturday.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Can a Friday T+1 U.S. equity trade settle on Saturday?
items.correction: Count the next eligible business day, Monday when no market holiday intervenes.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake: A trader may mistake the first calendar day after a Friday transaction for an eligible securities settlement day. Correct it by declaring the missing information and using only completed, reported evidence rather than inventing a fill.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: Under the same no-holiday T+1 example, what day follows a Thursday trade for settlement? Explain the relevant units, what is only assumed, and what would invalidate your result.
items.riskBoundary: Asset class, holidays, special terms can change dates.

items.title: Execution time and settlement time describe different stages of a transaction
items.specificTeachingObjective: A recorded trade execution and subsequent securities/cash settlement are separate operational events.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: An order fills on Tuesday at 10:15 a.m.; assuming no holiday and standard T+1, settlement is Wednesday, but the execution remains Tuesday at 10:15.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Should a Tuesday 10:15 execution be journaled as a Wednesday trade?
items.correction: Preserve executed timestamp on Tuesday; record settlement as a distinct Wednesday operational event.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake: A student may date the trade by settlement and distort their replay journal's actual decision time. Correct it by declaring the missing information and using only completed, reported evidence rather than inventing a fill.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: A completed Thursday fill at 2:00 p.m. with no intervening holiday has what assumed T+1 settlement date, and when was the fill? Explain the relevant units, what is only assumed, and what would invalidate your result.
items.riskBoundary: Settlement date is not evidence of when the fill was known.

items.title: Displayed order-book depth is not evidence that those shares traded
items.specificTeachingObjective: A book snapshot displays resting quoted interest, whereas traded volume reflects actual executed prints over a defined interval.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Two displayed bid levels show 300 and 200 shares, totaling 500 displayed bid shares; no traded share volume is established by this snapshot.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Did 500 displayed bid shares trade merely by appearing in Level II?
items.correction: Distinguish outstanding displayed orders from actual executed prints.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake: A tape learner may count every displayed bid order as a confirmed purchase. Correct it by declaring the missing information and using only completed, reported evidence rather than inventing a fill.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: A displayed ask shows 150 plus 250 shares; find displayed ask depth and explain whether a print occurred. Explain the relevant units, what is only assumed, and what would invalidate your result.
items.riskBoundary: Hidden/cancelled orders and feed snapshots are not fills.

items.title: Order count and displayed share quantity are separate market-depth measurements
items.specificTeachingObjective: One resting order can represent many shares, and several orders can together represent the same displayed quantity.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: One displayed bid order has 500 shares while five others each have 100; six orders together show 1,000 shares.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Does six displayed orders automatically mean six shares?
items.correction: Count the six orders and separately sum their 1,000 displayed shares.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake: A trader may see 1,000 shares and claim there were exactly 1,000 buyers. Correct it by declaring the missing information and using only completed, reported evidence rather than inventing a fill.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: Four bid orders each display 75 shares; state the order count and aggregate displayed share quantity. Explain the relevant units, what is only assumed, and what would invalidate your result.
items.riskBoundary: Aggregated-by-price depth may omit underlying order count.

items.title: A day-order duration does not establish whether an order executed
items.specificTeachingObjective: A day order's designated active interval and any completed execution are independent facts about order handling.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: A 100-share day limit order submitted at 3:45 p.m. has zero reported fills by the assumed 4:00 p.m. regular-session end; its executed share count remains 0.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Does a Day limit order prove all 100 shares filled by 4:00?
items.correction: Use broker-reported executed quantity and remaining unfilled status at cutoff.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake: A trader may mistake an expired order for a filled transaction because a later chart crossed the limit. Correct it by declaring the missing information and using only completed, reported evidence rather than inventing a fill.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: A 50-share day limit shows 20 shares filled before session end; how many actually executed, and what remains unfilled? Explain the relevant units, what is only assumed, and what would invalidate your result.
items.riskBoundary: Time-in-force expiration is not an execution record.

items.title: A pre-halt last price does not determine the price of a later reopening fill
items.specificTeachingObjective: When trading is halted, a previously reported last price is historical context, not a guaranteed executable quote at reopening.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: A stock last printed at $20.00 before a halt and a later documented reopening print is $18.40, a −8% print-to-print change.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Can a pre-halt $20 quote determine the reopening execution price?
items.correction: Only an actual later reopening print documents a retrospective $18.40 price.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake: A trader may mark a stopped strategy closed at the pre-halt quote despite no eligible execution. Correct it by declaring the missing information and using only completed, reported evidence rather than inventing a fill.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: The pre-halt last print is $30 and an observed reopening fill is $31.50; calculate the historical change without claiming a guaranteed price. Explain the relevant units, what is only assumed, and what would invalidate your result.
items.riskBoundary: Before the reopening, its price is future information.

items.title: Time-and-sales prints cannot identify the actual beneficial buyer by color
items.specificTeachingObjective: A transaction print reports executed quantity and price, but chart colors or bid/ask classifiers do not provide personal trader identity.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: A 500-share print at $12.10 appears while the quoted ask is $12.10; 500 traded shares are observed, but the print does not name 500 different buyers.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Does a red or green Time & Sales print reveal buyer identity?
items.correction: Observe print quantity and price; infer aggressor side only cautiously with matched quotes.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake: A trader may interpret a green tape entry as proof that a specific institution initiated a buy. Correct it by declaring the missing information and using only completed, reported evidence rather than inventing a fill.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: An observed 200-share print occurs at a displayed bid of $9.95; state the known execution quantity and what the color cannot prove. Explain the relevant units, what is only assumed, and what would invalidate your result.
items.riskBoundary: Color never proves beneficial ownership or count of counterparties.

items.title: Historical print reports can arrive later than the underlying execution time
items.specificTeachingObjective: A reported arrival timestamp and the actual trade timestamp can differ, especially after corrections or delayed reporting.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: A trade executed at 10:01:10 is reported at 10:01:25, fifteen seconds later; its availability to a 10:01:15 decision is not established by the later report.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Can a 10:01:25 reported print inform a 10:01:15 decision?
items.correction: Track execution time and separately received-at timestamp; no, it was not yet reported.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake: A replay learner may accidentally use a corrected historical print before the data was actually published. Correct it by declaring the missing information and using only completed, reported evidence rather than inventing a fill.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: A print executed at 09:35:00 reaches a feed at 09:35:12; calculate report latency and identify whether it was known at 09:35:05. Explain the relevant units, what is only assumed, and what would invalidate your result.
items.riskBoundary: Do not backdate late reports into earlier learning decisions.

items.title: Market-data aggregation changes what an interval-volume bar represents
items.specificTeachingObjective: A volume histogram bar aggregates prints attributed to a particular time interval, not individual order submissions.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Three prints of 100, 250 and 150 shares within a completed one-minute window produce a 500-share volume bar.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Can three executed prints be counted as one trade if they share a one-minute bar?
items.correction: Sum 100+250+150=500 shares but distinguish three prints from one volume bar.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake: A trader can misinterpret 500 share volume as 500 individual transactions or count future prints in an unfinished bar. Correct it by declaring the missing information and using only completed, reported evidence rather than inventing a fill.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: Four executions of 80, 120, 100 and 200 shares occur within one completed interval; compute its share-volume bar. Explain the relevant units, what is only assumed, and what would invalidate your result.
items.riskBoundary: Feed eligibility and corrections may modify aggregates.

items.title: Equal logarithmic price-axis spacing represents equal ratios rather than equal dollar moves
items.specificTeachingObjective: A logarithmic price axis compares relative price ratios, while a linear axis makes equal dollar differences equally tall.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Moving from $10 to $20 doubles price, as does moving from $20 to $40; both are 100% gains despite unequal $10 and $20 changes.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Do identical log-axis distances always represent identical dollar changes?
items.correction: Compare price ratios, such as $10→$20 versus $20→$40; both double.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake: A learner may judge two logarithmic candle distances as equal dollar profits instead of equal proportional changes. Correct it by declaring the missing information and using only completed, reported evidence rather than inventing a fill.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: Compare moves from $5 to $10 and $10 to $20 under a logarithmic axis and report each percentage change. Explain the relevant units, what is only assumed, and what would invalidate your result.
items.riskBoundary: Nonpositive prices cannot be represented by ordinary log scale.

items.title: A reported zero-volume interval is not evidence that price never moved in every venue
items.specificTeachingObjective: A zero in a specific feed's time bucket means no eligible counted executions were recorded there under that feed's inclusion rules.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: A chart feed records 0 eligible shares in one completed one-minute window and 600 in the next; the two buckets sum to 600 reported shares, not 600 trades.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Does a provider's zero-volume bar prove zero market movement everywhere?
items.correction: Interpret the zero only under the stated feed/session eligibility rule.
items.misconception: Live-trading mistake: A trader may fabricate activity by filling a missing bar with zero or assume all markets were inactive from one data provider's bucket. Correct it by declaring the missing information and using only completed, reported evidence rather than inventing a fill.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: Three completed buckets report 0, 150 and 250 shares; calculate reported share volume and identify what remains unknown. Explain the relevant units, what is only assumed, and what would invalidate your result.
items.riskBoundary: Explicit zero differs from missing observations and excluded venues.

items.title: A share repurchase and a cash dividend distribute value through different mechanisms
items.specificTeachingObjective: A cash dividend pays eligible holders directly, while a repurchase trades issuer cash for outstanding shares; effects depend on price, treasury treatment and later share count.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: A company has 1,000 shares and buys back 100 at $10 each for $1,000. If retired with no new shares, outstanding shares become 900; an unchanged holder with 90 shares moves from 9.00% to 10.00% ownership, but receives no dividend cash from that repurchase.
items.diagnosticQuestion: If 100 of 1,000 issuer shares are retired, does an unchanged 90-share holder receive cash?
items.correction: Their proportional share increases from 9% to 10% but they receive no dividend directly; firm value and retained-stock terms are separate.
items.misconception: Calling buyback spending a dividend paid to all shareholders or presuming a buyback always raises market price.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: With 2,000 shares outstanding, 200 are retired while a holder retains 100. Compute ownership before and after, without predicting price.
items.riskBoundary: The SEC May 2023 repurchase-disclosure modernization rule was vacated effective December 19, 2023. The archived SEC speech is history, not currently effective reporting requirements.

items.title: Preferred dividends and common voting claims are different security rights
items.specificTeachingObjective: Common and preferred shares may provide different voting, dividend and liquidation rights; issue terms, rather than the word preferred alone, govern priority.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: An issuer has common and noncumulative preferred stock with a contractual $2 preferred annual dividend. If no dividend is declared in one year, the student cannot assume a $2 arrear later; cumulative terms would be required for that conclusion.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Does an unpaid noncumulative preferred dividend automatically carry into the next year?
items.correction: No: the specified contractual cumulative or noncumulative terms control, and declaration is not universal.
items.misconception: Assuming every preferred issue votes like common stock or guarantees fixed cash regardless of board decisions.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: Compare two preferred series, one cumulative and one noncumulative, after two skipped $1 distributions. Describe contractual arrears conditionally.
items.riskBoundary: A preferred stock is not a guaranteed bond coupon; actual security terms determine priority, conversion, vote and liquidation.

items.title: A bond's stated maturity and its sensitivity to yield changes are different measurements
items.specificTeachingObjective: Maturity is a contractual calendar date; duration is an analytical measure of weighted cash-flow timing or yield sensitivity, with definitions that must be declared.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: Two securities each mature in five years, but one pays annual coupons and one pays no coupon. Their principal dates match; the coupon bond returns some cash earlier, so their Macaulay durations need not match five years.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Can a five-year coupon bond and five-year zero-coupon bond have identical duration by assumption?
items.correction: Compare timing of promised cashflows, not simply the shared legal maturity date; Macaulay duration is PV-weighted timing.
items.misconception: Treating 'five-year bond' as meaning a guaranteed 5% price movement for a one-point yield change.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: Compare a three-year zero-coupon bond with an otherwise similar annual-coupon bond. Which returns cash earlier?
items.riskBoundary: A bond's modified-duration estimate requires yield, convention and potentially option treatment; not a guaranteed rate-price forecast.

items.title: A squared-weight concentration index does not measure return covariance
items.specificTeachingObjective: A position-concentration index sums squared portfolio weights and describes capital allocation concentration, not how independently prices move.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: 50%,30%,20% weights give 0.50²+0.30²+0.20²=0.38; equal thirds would give 1/3≈0.333, showing greater concentration by this measure.
items.diagnosticQuestion: Does H=0.38 prove this portfolio is low-risk?
items.correction: No: sum squared portfolio weights measures concentration and gives an effective-holdings count of about 2.63; it does not measure covariance, leverage or future losses.
items.misconception: Treating several tickers or a low H score as evidence that prices cannot fall together.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: Calculate H for 50/50 and for four equal 25% positions; explain what H does not reveal.
items.riskBoundary: HHI portfolio weight convention uses decimal weights. Market-share HHI on a 0–10,000 regulatory scale is analogous, not identical. Concentration alone cannot guarantee risk reduction.

items.title: Fiscal statement dates are not equivalent to historical public-information timestamps
items.specificTeachingObjective: A financial statement describes a fiscal observation period; its filing/acceptance time controls when its particular disclosure could enter the public information set.
items.workedCase: FICTIONAL: A company's year ends December 31, but the annual filing is accepted by EDGAR on February 20, and its first public availability may occur later. A January 15 replay must not use that 10-K as known information merely because it reports the prior year.
items.diagnosticQuestion: If a Form 10-K has an EDGAR acceptance timestamp at 14:00, may a 14:00 historical replay use it as publicly known?
items.correction: No: acceptance is a different event from first public dissemination; SEC reports often 1–3 minutes lag but no exact first-public-availability timestamp. Use independently observed release or a conservatively declared lag.
items.misconception: Backdating financial information to period end and leaking unseen future filing facts into practice scenarios.
items.independentTransfer: FICTIONAL TRANSFER: A quarter ends June 30, filing occurs August 6. Could a July 10 replay cite its 10-Q figures?
items.riskBoundary: A December 31 fiscal period end is not public release; filing acceptance also cannot certify the first available second on SEC.gov.
